A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPHINX by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original particle simulations and NBA trajectory-prediction experiments, including structural recovery, ablations and slot-count sensitivity results.

after.justification: v2 retains original trajectory experiments and reports additional NTU and ModelNet40 classification results, predictor comparisons and quantitative analyses of inferred hypergraphs.

M1.justification: The sequential slot-attention predictor, binary history features, constrained k-subset sampling and hypergraph processing remain unchanged. Equations 1–2 and the decoder formulation match. The added classification experiments do not document a new algorithm or architectural component.

E1.justification: v2 adds transductive object classification on NTU and ModelNet40, substantially extending coverage beyond trajectory prediction. NBA is retained, while the reported synthetic evaluation concentrates on the former Two-Triangles setup, now called Particle Simulation; the separate One-Triangle evaluation is removed, although illustrative trajectories remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds GroupNet and TDHNN to the particle comparisons and TDHNN to both NBA comparison tables. The new classification comparison includes static and dynamic methods such as GCN, HGNN+, HNHN, HyperGCN, DHGNN, DeepHGSL and HSL. Conversely, v1's synthetic LSTM and ground-truth oracle comparisons are removed.

E3.justification: The added classification evaluation uses three feature configurations—GVCNN, MVCNN and their combination—and splits attributed to Zhou et al. v2 also specifies a common decoder for its added synthetic predictor comparisons and a six-hyperedge, four-node configuration for NBA structural analysis. The retained trajectory horizons and stated training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 retains the sequential-prediction, sampling and slot-count studies but substantially expands structural diagnostics: Figure 2b compares reconstruction overlap across predictors and ablations, Appendix D quantifies NBA node degrees and duplicate hyperedges, and Table 5 measures unique hyperedges under excess slots. The oracle-gap and LSTM temporal-degradation analyses from v1's Appendix D.1 are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates and plots without explicit repeated-run uncertainty. v2's new Table 2 reports means and standard deviations over 20 runs for classification. This introduces uncertainty reporting for those experiments without establishing additional runs or changed statistical practices for the retained trajectory results.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive classification results, including NTU/GVCNN scores of 94.80±0.90 for SPHINX and 92.70±1.61 for TDHNN*, plus new predictor and structural-diagnostic results. It reports 90% versus 67% synthetic overlap for SPHINX versus TDHNN. Retained NBA entries are unchanged. One-Triangle, LSTM and oracle result entries from v1 disappear.

T1.justification: The mathematical model, higher-order dynamics assumption, slot-update equations and permutation-matched overlap definition remain unchanged. The computational-complexity analysis moves from v1 Appendix C.2 to v2 Appendix C with the same bound. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The central method contribution is retained, but v2 broadens its principal empirical claims to both inductive trajectory prediction and transductive node classification. Its abstract and introduction explicitly claim superiority over existing hypergraph predictors, strengthening v1's claims of useful, interpretable latent structures and improved trajectory prediction.

C2.justification: v2 adds the qualification that annotated real-world hypergraphs need not be optimal for the downstream task and interprets TDHNN's dense structures as attention learning rather than useful sparse connectivity. It further interprets quantitative diversity and redundancy findings. Existing fixed-cardinality, maximum-slot and temporally static-structure limitations remain, while the oracle-performance-gap discussion is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds classification feature sources and split provenance, documents the shared-decoder baseline control and specifies the NBA structural-analysis configuration. It also promises a future full-code release, without providing a released SPHINX resource. The existing tuning grids, training details and dependency-code links are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around static versus learned structures and inductive versus transductive applicability. New Appendix B and Table 4 compare differentiability, discreteness and regularization requirements across predictors, incorporating works such as TDHNN, DynGroupNet, DeepHGSL and MHSL. Earlier discussion of differentiable cell complexes and supervised set-to-hypergraph inference is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially reframed around three design requirements, related work is rewritten, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around inductive and transductive settings. The appendix is restructured, including a separate complexity section and predictor overview, although much of the method and limitations prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from one to two columns, reformats and transposes the NBA tables, and combines revised performance plots, a new overlap panel and the retained decoder-learning curves into Figure 2. It adds classification, predictor-overview and unique-hyperedge tables while removing the detailed synthetic result tables. Several appendix graphics are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v1's broad applicability claim was supported principally by trajectory tasks and limited direct predictor comparisons. v2 substantially strengthens that foundation through transductive classification, controlled predictor comparisons, 20-run uncertainty reporting and quantitative structural diagnostics. Removing the oracle/LSTM comparisons and exact synthetic tables reduces diagnostic transparency, and the broader superiority wording exceeds the mixed long-horizon NBA rankings. Nevertheless, the new evidence meaningfully addresses the earlier validation gap and yields a substantial net improvement.
